Check The Evidence Behind The Working Labels
The working interpretations above should not be read as automatic names. They are short labels for evidence patterns. A label is strongest when two kinds of evidence agree:

local model evidence, such as stimulation correlation, dominant cell-type activity, top genes, and expression direction; and
prior biological knowledge, such as known interferon-stimulated genes, antigen-presentation genes, or immune-cell annotations from the source study.

This distinction matters because not all six labels have the same strength. Some are gene-anchored: the top genes have a well-established biological role. Others are more activity-anchored: the pattern is strongest in a particular annotated cell population, but the top genes are not enough by themselves to name a pathway.

Pattern4, broad IFN-associated stimulation, has the strongest support. It has high stimulation correlation, a large positive stimulated-minus-control activity shift, mostly up-regulated top genes, and top genes such as ISG15, ISG20, IFI6, IFIT3, IFIT1, MX1, OAS1, and IRF7. Those genes are consistent with the IFN-beta perturbation in the source study and with the interferon-stimulated gene biology introduced in the Context section (Kang et al. 2018; Chyuan, Tzeng, and Chen 2019; Catalina et al. 2019).
Pattern5, monocyte-biased stimulation-linked, has a moderate positive stimulation association and many stimulation-up genes, including interferon-related genes. Its “monocyte-biased” part comes from the local activity evidence: the pattern is strongest in annotated CD14+ monocytes. That is why the label is more cautious than Pattern4. It suggests an IFN-responsive signal with stronger monocyte activity, not a fully separate monocyte pathway.
Pattern3, dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked, is strongly supported by its top genes. CD74 and HLA class II genes such as HLA-DRA, HLA-DRB1, HLA-DPA1, and HLA-DPB1 are tied to MHC class II antigen processing and presentation (Blum, Wearsch, and Cresswell 2013). The local activity evidence adds that this pattern is strongest in annotated dendritic cells, a blood immune-cell population where antigen-presentation biology is expected (Villani et al. 2017).
Pattern1 and Pattern2, monocyte-linked, are mainly activity-anchored. Pattern1 is strongest in annotated FCGR3A+ monocytes and includes FCGR3A among its top genes. Pattern2 is strongest in annotated CD14+ monocytes, but its top genes include several broad baseline or stress-response genes, such as ferritin genes. Human blood monocytes are often discussed using CD14/CD16-related distinctions, and single-cell blood atlases show that monocyte and dendritic-cell annotations can contain multiple related subtypes (Ziegler-Heitbrock et al. 2010; Villani et al. 2017). In this table, those labels should therefore be read as “where the pattern is strongest,” not as complete pathway names.
Pattern6, T-cell / lymphocyte-linked baseline, is also activity-anchored. It is strongest in annotated CD4 T cells and has lower activity after stimulation, but its top genes are not a clean T-cell receptor or cytokine pathway. The safest interpretation is that this pattern marks lymphocyte-neighborhood baseline structure in this run. This is still useful, because a latent model can contain both cell-identity-like signals and cell-activity-like signals in the same dataset (Kotliar et al. 2019).

Taken together, the selected model does not recover only one stimulation signal. It contains a strongly supported IFN-associated stimulation pattern, a second more cautious monocyte-biased stimulation-linked pattern, a gene-anchored antigen-presentation-linked pattern, and several activity-anchored immune-cell-linked baseline patterns. The next questions test the most important part of that inventory more deeply: whether the IFN-associated pattern behaves like a broad stimulation response rather than a mislabeled cell-type pattern.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Finding latent immune-response programs in single-cell RNA-seq with CoGAPS
section: Question 2: Can CoGAPS Separate Stimulation From Cell-Type-Linked Structure?
text:
Question 2: Can CoGAPS Separate Stimulation From Cell-Type-Linked Structure?
This question asks whether the selected model contains a broad IFN-beta stimulation signal while still retaining immune-cell-linked structure. You answer it by testing the paired stimulation shift, comparing the IFN-associated pattern with a simple interferon-stimulated gene score, and contrasting that pattern with an antigen-presentation-linked pattern.
Here, compare means asking whether two different kinds of evidence point to the same biological signal. If the IFN-associated CoGAPS pattern rises after stimulation and also agrees with a simple interferon-stimulated gene score, that supports interpreting the pattern as an IFN-beta response rather than as a numerical pattern with no clear biology.
Here, contrast means setting that IFN-associated pattern beside a different pattern that should behave differently. An An immune process in which cells display peptide fragments on major histocompatibility complex molecules so T cells can inspect them.antigen-presentation-linked pattern, for example, may be defined by CD74 and HLA class II genes rather than by a broad stimulation shift. Seeing those differences helps you separate a shared treatment-response signal from immune-cell-linked biology (Blum, Wearsch, and Cresswell 2013).

Test The Paired IFN Activity Shift
The source experiment used a A design in which related samples are compared, such as control and stimulated aliquots from the same donor.paired design: each donor contributed a control aliquot and an IFN-beta-stimulated aliquot. That design is valuable because each donor can serve as their own comparison. Instead of asking only whether all stimulated cells have higher activity on average, you can ask whether the shift appears within each matched donor pair.
The code below filters to the IFN-associated pattern, separates control and stimulated mean activity by donor, computes stim - control, and then performs a one-sided A simple paired test that counts how often the direction of change is the same across matched pairs.sign test. The sign test asks a simple question: if stimulation had no consistent direction, how surprising would it be to see this many donor pairs shift upward?

RPython



ifn_replicate_r <- activity_by_replicate_r |>
  dplyr::filter(pattern == ifn_pattern_r)

ctrl_replicate_r <- ifn_replicate_r |>
  dplyr::filter(condition == "ctrl") |>
  dplyr::select(replicate, ctrl_mean_activity = mean_activity, ctrl_n_cells = n_cells)

stim_replicate_r <- ifn_replicate_r |>
  dplyr::filter(condition == "stim") |>
  dplyr::select(replicate, stim_mean_activity = mean_activity, stim_n_cells = n_cells)

ifn_pair_shift_r <- dplyr::inner_join(
  ctrl_replicate_r,
  stim_replicate_r,
  by = "replicate"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(activity_shift = stim_mean_activity - ctrl_mean_activity)

n_positive_r <- sum(ifn_pair_shift_r$activity_shift > 0)
n_nonzero_r <- sum(ifn_pair_shift_r$activity_shift != 0)
sign_test_r <- binom.test(
  n_positive_r,
  n_nonzero_r,

def one_sided_sign_test_pvalue(n_positive, n_nonzero):
    """Exact one-sided sign-test probability under a 50/50 null."""
    return sum(comb(n_nonzero, k) for k in range(n_positive, n_nonzero + 1)) / (2 ** n_nonzero)

Read the table as a donor-paired direction check, not as a cell-level test. Each donor contributes one matched comparison: the mean IFN-associated pattern activity in that donor’s stimulated aliquot minus the mean activity in that donor’s control aliquot.

IFN-associated pattern gives the run-specific pattern label being tested. In the selected R run, this is Pattern4; in another run, the same biological signal can have a different pattern number.
Matched donor pairs is the number of donors that have both a control and stimulated measurement available for this comparison.
Pairs higher after stimulation counts how many donor pairs have a positive stim - control shift. Here, 8 means every matched donor pair moved in the same upward direction.
Mean shift and median shift summarize the size of the donor-level activity change. The mean is the average shift across donors; the median is the middle donor shift and is less sensitive to one unusually large or small donor response.
One-sided sign-test p-value asks how surprising it would be to observe at least this many upward shifts if upward and downward shifts were equally likely. With 8 of 8 donor pairs higher after stimulation, the probability under that no-direction null is 0.00391, or about 0.4%.

The p-value comes from the directions of the paired shifts, not from thousands of individual cells and not from the size of the shifts. That is why the table reports both pieces of evidence: the sign test checks whether the direction is consistent across donors, while the mean and median shifts show how large the activity change is on the CoGAPS activity scale.
For the selected R run, all eight matched donor pairs have higher IFN-associated activity after stimulation. The Python-compatible output shows the same qualitative result for its matched IFN-associated pattern. This is stronger evidence than a pooled cell-level average because it respects the paired study design.
The sign test is intentionally modest. It does not claim that IFN-beta stimulation has the same effect size in every donor, and it does not replace a full clinical model. It simply checks whether the direction of the pattern activity shift is consistent across the donor pairs in this dataset.


Optional Formal Check: Account For Donor With A Mixed Model
The paired sign test checks whether the direction of change is consistent across donors. A A statistical model that estimates an overall effect while accounting for grouped or repeated measurements, such as control and stimulated samples from the same donor.mixed model asks a slightly different question: after allowing each donor to have their own baseline activity, is the average stimulation effect still positive?
This is useful because donors can differ before stimulation. One donor may have higher baseline pattern activity than another donor even before IFN-beta is added. If you ignore that pairing, the analysis can mix two ideas together: differences between donors and the effect of stimulation within the same donor.
The model below separates those ideas. It treats condition as the effect of interest: stimulated versus control. It treats donor as the grouping term: measurements from the same donor are related because they come from matched aliquots. In plain language, the model asks:

After accounting for each donor’s baseline activity level, how much higher is the IFN-associated pattern activity in stimulated aliquots than in control aliquots?

The model is fit to donor-level mean activity, not to every cell. In this dataset, that means each donor contributes one control mean and one stimulated mean for the IFN-associated pattern. This keeps the analysis aligned with the experimental design and avoids treating thousands of cells as thousands of independent donors.
The R and Python chunks below do the same analysis in parallel:

They start from the donor-by-condition activity table for the IFN-associated pattern.
They keep only the columns needed for the model: donor, condition, and mean activity.
They make control the reference condition, so the stimulation coefficient is interpreted as stim - control.
They fit a random-intercept mixed model. In R, nlme::lme(mean_activity ~ condition, random = ~ 1 | replicate) means “estimate the condition effect, while allowing each donor to have its own baseline.” In Python, statsmodels uses the same idea with mean_activity ~ condition_stim and groups = replicate.
They extract the stimulation effect, its uncertainty, the p-value, and the variation left over after accounting for condition and donor.
They place those quantities into a small summary table so the statistical result can be read beside the simpler paired sign-test result.

Read this model as a formal companion to the sign test, not as a separate discovery. The sign test used only the direction of each donor-pair shift. The mixed model uses the donor-level activity values themselves while still accounting for the fact that control and stimulated measurements are paired within donor.
Here is how to read the mixed-model table:

IFN-associated pattern gives the run-specific pattern label being tested. In the selected R run, this is Pattern4.
Model question states the comparison being estimated: stimulated mean activity versus control mean activity, while accounting for donor.
Estimated stimulation effect is the estimated average stim - control difference after the model accounts for donor baselines. A positive value means stimulated aliquots have higher IFN-associated activity on average. Here, 0.281 is nearly identical to the simple donor-paired mean shift above, which is reassuring.
Standard error summarizes the uncertainty around that estimated stimulation effect. A small standard error relative to the estimate means the donor-level shifts are very consistent.
T statistic in R, or z statistic in Python, is the estimated stimulation effect divided by its standard error. A large positive value means the estimated stimulation effect is much larger than its estimated uncertainty.
P-value tests the model-based null idea that the average stimulation effect is zero after accounting for donor. The value <0.001 is consistent with a strong positive stimulation-associated shift in this dataset.
Donor baseline SD summarizes how much the fitted donor baselines vary after condition is included. A value near zero means the donor-level baseline differences are small in this summarized table.
Residual SD summarizes the remaining donor-condition variation after the model accounts for condition and donor. Smaller residual variation means the donor-level points sit close to the fitted model.

The main result is the estimated stimulation effect. A positive effect of about 0.281 means that, after donor pairing is accounted for, the selected R IFN-associated pattern has higher average activity in IFN-beta-stimulated aliquots than in matched control aliquots. This points in the same direction as the paired sign test, which strengthens the conclusion that the IFN-associated activity shift is not caused by one donor alone.
With only eight donor pairs, the p-value should still be interpreted as a compact check inside this dataset rather than as a broad clinical inference. The useful message is the agreement across evidence types: paired direction, estimated effect size, and biological gene support all point toward the same stimulation-associated pattern.


Compare Activity With A Canonical ISG Score
The IFN-associated pattern should not only separate stimulated and control cells. Its activity should also agree with known interferon biology. One simple way to check that is to build a small score from canonical A gene whose expression can change when a cell responds to interferon signaling.interferon-stimulated genes, often called ISGs.
This is a teaching check, not a new cell-type annotation. The short list below is a compact guidepost drawn from interferon-response resources rather than a new signature discovered in this case study. Many of the genes appear in the MSigDB Hallmark interferon-response gene sets, and Interferome provides a broader catalog of interferon-regulated genes (Liberzon et al. 2015; Rusinova et al. 2013). The Kang source study supplies the IFN-beta PBMC perturbation context, while the lupus/interferon literature explains why an interferon-gene score is relevant in SLE (Kang et al. 2018; Catalina et al. 2019; Chyuan, Tzeng, and Chen 2019).
The code below turns that biological guidepost into a small, checkable table. Both tabs do the same four things. First, the code defines the compact ISG list. Second, it checks which of those genes are actually present in the prepared single-cell dataset. Third, it averages the expression of the available ISGs within each cell, producing one ISG score per cell. Fourth, it compares that per-cell ISG score with the run-specific IFN-associated CoGAPS activity. In the selected R run, that activity comes from Pattern4; in the Python output, it comes from the matched IFN-associated pattern for that implementation.
In the R tab, intersect() keeps only genes that appear in both the ISG list and the SingleCellExperiment row names. SummarizedExperiment::assay(sce_cells, "X") pulls out the prepared expression matrix, and colMeans() averages the selected ISG expression values across genes for each cell. The final cor(..., method = "spearman") call compares ranked ISG scores with ranked CoGAPS activity values, so the check asks whether cells with higher ISG expression also tend to have higher IFN-associated pattern activity.
The Python tab follows the same logic with AnnData and pandas. A list comprehension keeps genes found in adata_cells.var_names, slicing adata_cells[:, isg_genes_present].X pulls out the expression values, and mean(axis=1) averages those genes within each cell. The .rank().corr(...) step performs the same Spearman-style comparison by correlating the ranks of the ISG score and the ranks of the IFN-associated pattern activity.

Test Targeted IFN And Antigen-Presentation Gene-Set Support
Top genes are easier to interpret when they are checked against known biological gene sets. Here we use two small targeted sets:

an IFN / antiviral response set, which includes common interferon-stimulated genes; and
an antigen-presentation set, which includes CD74 and HLA class II genes. HLA-DR, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DP are human MHC class II molecules, and CD74 is the invariant chain involved in MHC class II assembly and trafficking, so this compact set is a transparent marker for antigen-presentation biology (Blum, Wearsch, and Cresswell 2013).

This is not a full pathway database analysis. It is a transparent targeted A check for whether genes from a biological reference set appear more often in a selected gene list than expected by chance.enrichment check. The code asks whether each pattern’s top 50 genes contain more genes from a small reference set than expected from the 3,000-gene modeling universe.
The basic idea is a counting comparison. For each CoGAPS pattern, the code takes the 50 genes with the largest pattern weights. It then asks how many of those 50 genes overlap a targeted reference set. If many IFN / antiviral genes appear among a pattern’s top 50 genes, that pattern has interferon-response gene support. If many antigen-presentation genes appear among a pattern’s top 50 genes, that pattern has antigen-presentation gene support.
The p-value in this table is an overlap probability. It asks: if you drew 50 genes from the 3,000 modeled genes, how surprising would it be to see at least this many genes from the targeted set? In R, fisher.test(..., alternative = "greater") computes that one-sided overlap test from a small 2-by-2 contingency table. In Python, the helper function hypergeom_tail() computes the same kind of upper-tail probability directly from combinations.
Several programming moves are worth noticing. Both tabs define two named gene sets, define the modeling universe as the genes in the CoGAPS gene-weight matrix, loop across patterns, select each pattern’s top 50 genes, count overlaps with each targeted gene set, and then assemble one summary row per pattern and gene set. The R code stores rows in a list of small tibbles and combines them with dplyr::bind_rows(). The Python code stores dictionaries in a list and turns them into a pandas DataFrame.

def hypergeom_tail(overlap, set_size, draws, universe_size):
    """Probability of seeing at least this overlap by chance."""
    max_overlap = min(set_size, draws)
    denominator = comb(universe_size, draws)
    numerator = 0
    for k in range(overlap, max_overlap + 1):
        if draws - k <= universe_size - set_size:
            numerator += comb(set_size, k) * comb(universe_size - set_size, draws - k)
    return numerator / denominator

    top_genes = set(A_py[pattern].sort_values(ascending=False).head(top_n_gene_set).index)
    for gene_set_name, genes in target_gene_sets.items():
        set_genes = set(genes).intersection(gene_universe)
        overlap_genes = sorted(top_genes.intersection(set_genes))
        p_value = hypergeom_tail(
            overlap=len(overlap_genes),
            set_size=len(set_genes),
            draws=top_n_gene_set,
            universe_size=len(gene_universe),
        )
        gene_set_records.append(
            {
                "Pattern": pattern,
                "Targeted gene set": gene_set_name,
                "Set genes present": len(set_genes),
                "Top-50 overlap": len(overlap_genes),
                "Example overlapping genes": ", ".join(overlap_genes[:8]),
                "Enrichment p-value": p_value,
            }
        )

targeted_gene_set_results = (
    pd.DataFrame(gene_set_records)
    .sort_values(["Targeted gene set", "Enrichment p-value"])
)

targeted_gene_set_display = targeted_gene_set_results.copy()
targeted_gene_set_display["Enrichment p-value"] = targeted_gene_set_display[
    "Enrichment p-value"
].apply(lambda p: "<0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3g}")

print(render_table(targeted_gene_set_display))

Here is how to read the table. Pattern is the run-specific CoGAPS label. Targeted gene set tells you which reference list is being checked. Set genes present is the number of genes from that reference list that are available in the 3,000-gene modeling space. Top-50 overlap counts how many of those genes appear among the 50 highest-weight genes for that pattern. Example overlapping genes shows some of the actual genes driving the overlap. Enrichment p-value summarizes how surprising that overlap would be if the top 50 genes were drawn without regard to the targeted biology.
The IFN / antiviral rows show that interferon-response genes are concentrated in stimulation-linked patterns. In the selected R run, the IFN-associated pattern, Pattern4, has 16 of the 17 targeted IFN / antiviral genes among its top 50 genes. Pattern5 also has strong IFN / antiviral gene support, which is why it was described earlier as monocyte-biased stimulation-linked rather than ignored. This is a useful reminder that gene-set support does not name a pattern by itself. The broader interpretation still depends on the activity evidence: Pattern4 is the broad IFN-associated pattern because it combines IFN-linked genes with the strongest stimulation correlation and paired donor shift.
The antigen-presentation rows give a different kind of evidence. In the selected R run, Pattern3 has the strongest antigen-presentation support, with 8 of the 10 targeted antigen-presentation genes among its top 50 genes. The overlapping genes include CD74 and HLA class II genes such as HLA-DRA, HLA-DRB1, HLA-DPA1, and HLA-DPB1. That result supports using Pattern3 as a contrast pattern: it looks less like a broad IFN-beta stimulation response and more like dendritic-cell / antigen-presentation-linked structure.
The main takeaway is not that one p-value settles the biology. Instead, the targeted gene-set check adds a second layer of evidence to the earlier activity summaries. It shows that the model contains both interferon-response gene structure and non-IFN immune structure, which is exactly what you need if the goal is to separate stimulation-associated activity from cell-type-linked biology.


Use An Identity-Linked Pattern As A Contrast
It is tempting to focus only on the IFN-associated pattern, but that would miss an important lesson. A good latent-variable analysis should also ask what the other patterns capture. The targeted gene-set check above points to an antigen-presentation-linked pattern whose top genes include CD74 and HLA class II genes. This pattern is useful as a contrast because it looks more like immune-cell identity or antigen-presentation structure than a broad stimulation response.
The code below selects the pattern with the strongest antigen-presentation targeted enrichment and summarizes its top genes and direction. This gives you a second example of why CoGAPS gene weights and expression direction should be interpreted together.
The selection step uses the targeted gene-set table you just created. It keeps only the rows for the antigen-presentation gene set, sorts those rows by enrichment p-value, and takes the top row. That top row gives the pattern whose highest-weight genes are most enriched for the targeted antigen-presentation markers. After that, the code goes back to the directionality table, keeps only genes from that selected pattern, sorts them by CoGAPS gene-weight rank, and prints the first 12 genes.
In the R tab, filter() keeps the antigen-presentation rows, arrange() puts the smallest p-value first, slice(1) keeps the strongest row, and pull(pattern) extracts the pattern label as a single value. The next pipe uses that label to filter direction_global_r, then formats the log2 fold-change and pair-consistency columns for display. In the Python tab, the same idea is written with pandas: .loc[...] keeps antigen-presentation rows, .sort_values(...) orders them by p-value, .iloc[0] takes the first pattern label, and the second method chain filters direction_global to the selected pattern.

Here is how to read the table. Rank orders genes by their CoGAPS weight within the selected antigen-presentation-linked pattern. Gene names the feature being inspected. CoGAPS weight tells you how strongly that gene helps define the pattern. Mean log2FC: IFN-beta vs control is the paired expression contrast: positive values mean the gene is higher after stimulation, while negative values mean it is lower after stimulation. Direction turns that contrast into a readable label. Pair consistency summarizes how consistently the direction appears across donor pairs. Evidence strength is a compact label from the prepared directionality summary.
The antigen-presentation-linked pattern has a different biological role from the IFN-associated pattern. Its top genes help mark antigen-presentation biology, especially MHC class II-related structure. That matters because PBMC data contain immune-cell identity structure before any stimulation comparison is made. A dendritic-cell-associated pattern can be biologically meaningful even if it is not the strongest IFN-beta response.
This contrast also protects the IFN interpretation from becoming too broad. The IFN-associated pattern is supported by a stimulation shift, an ISG-score correlation, and IFN / antiviral top genes. The antigen-presentation-linked pattern is supported by a different kind of evidence: antigen-presentation genes and identity-linked activity. Seeing both kinds of patterns in the same selected model supports the idea that CoGAPS is separating at least two useful layers of the PBMC data: a broad stimulation-associated layer and a cell-identity-linked immune-function layer.


Question 2 Answer: Broad Stimulation And Identity-Linked Structure Are Both Present
Question 2 asked whether CoGAPS can help distinguish broad stimulation-associated activity from cell-type-linked immune programs. The evidence in this section supports a cautious yes.
The paired donor test showed that the IFN-associated pattern is higher after IFN-beta stimulation in all eight matched donor pairs. The mixed model reached the same conclusion while accounting for donor baselines. The ISG-score check showed that cells with higher IFN-associated CoGAPS activity also tend to have higher expression of a compact interferon-stimulated gene score. The targeted gene-set check then connected the same pattern to IFN / antiviral genes among its highest-weight genes.
The contrast pattern adds the other half of the answer. The model does not only contain a stimulation signal. It also contains a pattern whose evidence points toward dendritic-cell / antigen-presentation-linked biology. That is important because the PBMC mixture is not a blank background. It contains immune-cell identities, and a useful latent-variable model should preserve some of that structure rather than forcing every signal to be interpreted as stimulation.
Together, these checks show why the case study does not rely on one diagnostic alone. A stimulation-associated pattern should be active in the expected cells, shift in the expected condition, agree with known interferon biology, and have genes that support the interpretation. A cell-identity-linked pattern should have a different evidence profile. With that distinction in place, the next question turns from where the IFN-associated pattern is active to which genes define it and whether those genes rise or fall after stimulation.

section: Question 3: Which Genes Define The IFN-Associated Pattern, And In Which Direction?
text:
Question 3: Which Genes Define The IFN-Associated Pattern, And In Which Direction?
This question asks which genes make the IFN-associated pattern interpretable and whether those genes are higher or lower after stimulation. That distinction matters because CoGAPS gene weights identify genes that define a pattern, while expression contrasts identify direction.

Inspect Direction Within The IFN-Associated Pattern
Now return to the key point from the visualization section: CoGAPS weights and expression direction are different quantities. A high gene weight means the gene helps define the pattern. Whether expression is higher or lower in one condition compared with another.Directionality asks whether the gene is higher or lower after IFN-beta stimulation.
The table below focuses on the top genes from the IFN-associated pattern. It shows their CoGAPS weight alongside a donor-aware A summary that combines single-cell counts within a group, such as donor and condition, so expression differences can be compared at a grouped-sample level.pseudobulk log2 fold-change. Pseudobulk means that the single-cell counts are first added up within a meaningful group, such as one donor’s control cells or the same donor’s stimulated cells, before conditions are compared. That keeps the paired donor design visible and avoids treating thousands of cells from the same donor as thousands of independent donors.
The directionality summaries were generated before this section from the saved selected-model outputs and the count layer in the prepared PBMC dataset. The workflow did five things:

extracted the top genes for each CoGAPS pattern from the gene-weight matrix,
aggregated raw counts for those genes by donor and condition,
converted each pseudobulk profile to counts per million, or CPM, so groups with different total counts are more comparable,
computed log2(stimulated CPM + 0.5) - log2(control CPM + 0.5) for each donor pair, and
summarized the mean direction, pair consistency, and adjusted Wilcoxon evidence for each pattern gene.

The + 0.5 term is a small pseudocount. It prevents zeros from causing undefined logarithms. A positive mean log2 fold-change means the gene is higher after IFN-beta stimulation; a negative value means it is lower after stimulation.


Reproducibility note


The main analysis path reads saved directionality tables. To regenerate them in the validated environment, use the scripts listed in the Full Reproduction Guide:
Rscript scripts/pattern_directionality_analysis_r.R
python scripts/pattern_directionality_analysis.py
These scripts write the R and Python directionality summaries under data/processed/selected_model_k6/. They perform a targeted directionality analysis for top CoGAPS pattern genes; they are not a genome-wide differential-expression workflow.


The R and Python chunks below do the same display task. They do not recompute pseudobulk counts. Instead, each chunk starts from the saved global directionality table, keeps the run-specific IFN-associated pattern, orders genes by CoGAPS rank, rounds the numeric columns for reading, and prints the top 15 genes. This is a useful programming pattern: load a larger result table once, then filter and format the rows needed for the current question.

RPython


In R, dplyr::filter() keeps only the IFN-associated pattern from the selected R run. arrange(rank) restores the CoGAPS gene-weight order, so the highest-weight gene appears first. The mutate() step rounds values for display, and select() keeps only the columns needed to answer the question.

  dplyr::arrange(rank) |>

    sign_consistency = round(sign_consistency, 2),
    wilcoxon_fdr = signif(wilcoxon_fdr, 3)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    rank,
    gene,
    cogaps_weight,
    mean_log2fc_stim_vs_ctrl,
    direction,
    sign_consistency,
    evidence_strength,
    wilcoxon_fdr
  )

The one exception among the top 15 is FTH1, which has a high pattern weight but is lower after stimulation in this targeted summary.
That exception is important rather than problematic. It shows why the analysis keeps gene weight and expression direction separate. CoGAPS says that FTH1 helps define the pattern; the pseudobulk contrast says that its expression moves opposite the main ISG group after stimulation. A careful interpretation therefore describes the IFN-associated pattern as dominated by up-shifted interferon-stimulated genes, while noting that not every high-weight gene is up-regulated.

section: Question 4: How Does The IFN-Associated Pattern Vary Across PBMC Identities?
text:
Question 4: How Does The IFN-Associated Pattern Vary Across PBMC Identities?
This question asks whether the IFN-associated signal is broad across the PBMC mixture or mostly driven by one annotated immune-cell identity. The next check keeps the same IFN-associated top genes but summarizes their stimulation direction inside each annotated PBMC identity.

Check Whether The Direction Holds Across PBMC Identities
The IFN-associated pattern is broad, but PBMCs are a mixture of immune-cell identities. A responsible analysis asks whether the same direction appears across those identities or whether the global result is driven by one large cell type.
The next summary counts, within each annotated PBMC identity, how many of the IFN-associated pattern’s top genes are higher in stimulation, lower in stimulation, or mixed/unclear. The code uses group_by() and summarise() in R, and groupby() with size() in Python. These methods are common data-analysis skills: they split a table into groups, compute a summary inside each group, and return a smaller table.

RPython



ifn_direction_by_celltype_r <- direction_celltype_r |>
  dplyr::filter(pattern == ifn_pattern_r) |>
  dplyr::group_by(cell_type, direction) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_genes = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(
  ifn_direction_by_celltype_r,
  aes(x = cell_type, y = n_genes, fill = direction)
) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "up_in_stim" = "#E76F51",
      "down_in_stim" = "#2F8FBD",
      "mixed_or_unclear" = "#9CA3AF"
    ),
    breaks = c("up_in_stim", "down_in_stim", "mixed_or_unclear"),
    labels = c("higher in stimulation", "lower in stimulation", "mixed or unclear")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "IFN-associated top genes mostly rise across PBMC identities",
    x = "Annotated PBMC identity",
    y = "Number of top pattern genes",
    fill = "Expression direction"
  ) +

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Finding latent immune-response programs in single-cell RNA-seq with CoGAPS
text:
Pull The Evidence Together
The four main research questions are now connected to specific evidence. The table below makes that map explicit before the final synthesis.








Main research question
Evidence used in this section
Current answer




1. What latent transcriptional programs are present?
R/Python pattern matching, candidate-program inventory, targeted gene-set checks, and identity-linked contrast.
The selected model contains a strong IFN-associated pattern plus additional immune-cell-linked structure, including antigen-presentation-linked biology.


2. Can CoGAPS distinguish broad stimulation-associated activity from cell-type-linked immune programs?
Donor-paired IFN activity shift, donor-adjusted mixed-model check, canonical ISG-score agreement, IFN/antiviral enrichment, antigen-presentation enrichment, and identity-linked contrast.
Yes, the evidence supports a broad stimulation-associated signal while retaining non-IFN immune structure.


3. Which genes define the strongest IFN-associated pattern, and what is their direction in stimulation?
IFN-associated gene weights paired with donor-aware pseudobulk directionality.
Top genes such as ISG15, IFI6, IFIT3, IFIT1, MX1, OAS1, and BST2 define the pattern and are mostly higher after IFN-beta stimulation.


4. How does the IFN-associated pattern vary across annotated PBMC cell types?
Cell-type-stratified direction summaries for the IFN-associated pattern’s top genes.
The IFN-associated direction is broadly visible across annotated PBMC identities, with room for differences in response strength across cell types.



Taken together, these checks support a coherent interpretation rather than a single-metric label. The selected R model has enough diagnostic support to interpret cautiously: the chi-square trace reaches a plateau-like region, the snapshot checks show stable top genes for the major patterns, and the posterior uncertainty summaries do not suggest that the IFN-associated pattern is too unstable to use. Those checks do not prove that K = 6 is universally best. They do support using this selected model to ask the biological questions posed in the case study.
The first answer is that the model contains more than one kind of latent structure. The IFN-associated pattern is the clearest stimulation-linked signal: in the selected R run it is Pattern4, and in the Python saved output it is Pattern5. The number changes because CoGAPS pattern labels are run-specific, but the evidence points to the same biological signal: high activity after IFN-beta stimulation, high agreement with an interferon-stimulated gene score, and top genes such as ISG15, IFI6, IFIT3, IFIT1, MX1, OAS1, and BST2. The model also retains immune-cell-linked patterns, including monocyte-linked structure, a dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked pattern, and a T-cell / lymphocyte-linked baseline pattern. That matters because the analysis is not simply rediscovering “stimulated versus control”; it is separating stimulation-associated activity from other structure already present in the PBMC mixture.
The second answer is that the stimulation-associated signal is broad, but not identical in every cell type. The donor-paired analysis shows higher IFN-associated activity after stimulation in all eight matched donor pairs, and the mixed model reaches the same conclusion while accounting for donor baselines. The visualization section prepared the same idea visually: the UMAP activity maps showed that this pattern cuts across the cell-identity map rather than sitting in only one neighborhood. The cell-type-stratified summaries then showed that annotated PBMC identities can share the IFN-associated direction while still differing in response strength. This is the useful middle ground for a mixed immune-cell dataset: a shared perturbation response can be visible without erasing cell identity.
The third answer is that CoGAPS gene weights and expression direction have to be read together. The top genes for the IFN-associated pattern are strongly consistent with interferon biology, but the weights alone only say that those genes help define the pattern. The pseudobulk directionality summaries add the missing piece: among the top IFN-associated genes, most are higher after IFN-beta stimulation, while an exception such as FTH1 shows why direction cannot be assumed from the CoGAPS weight. The identity-linked contrast reinforces the same lesson. A dendritic / antigen-presentation-linked pattern can be defined by genes such as CD74 and HLA class II genes without behaving like the broad IFN-associated stimulation pattern.
The fourth answer is that the IFN-associated pattern varies across annotated PBMC identities in a biologically interpretable way. PBMCs contain T cells, B cells, NK cells, monocytes, dendritic cells, and smaller related populations. The lupus and interferon literature discussed in the context section makes this mixture important: type I interferon biology can connect multiple immune-cell populations through interferon-stimulated genes, antigen presentation, monocyte and dendritic-cell activity, and lymphocyte responses. In this dataset, the controlled IFN-beta stimulation lets you see one part of that biology under an experimental perturbation. The CoGAPS result is consistent with a shared interferon-response program layered on top of immune-cell identity.
The conclusion is therefore bounded but useful. For this public PBMC perturbation dataset from lupus donors, the selected R K = 6 sparse CoGAPS model is suitable for interpreting the main case-study question. It recovers a broad IFN-beta-associated pattern, preserves additional immune-cell-linked structure, and links the IFN-associated pattern to both expected interferon-stimulated genes and upward expression direction after stimulation. The result should not be read as a clinical lupus mechanism, a treatment analysis, or proof that the same numbered pattern will appear in every run. It does show that latent-pattern analysis can help separate a shared interferon-response signal from cell identity in a mixed immune-cell system, which is the key analysis skill this case study is designed to teach.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Finding latent immune-response programs in single-cell RNA-seq with CoGAPS
text:
Synopsis

In this case study, we used a processed PBMC single-cell RNA-seq dataset with control and IFN-beta stimulated cells to learn how a latent-variable method can reveal transcriptional programs that cut across cell-type labels.
We inspected the processed single-cell object, summarized condition and cell-type metadata, prepared a genes x cells CoGAPS input, and loaded selected R-primary CoGAPS artifacts. The rank K = 6 was selected before the main learner workflow using a limited model-selection sweep and follow-up pattern-structure comparison. Learners do not need to run that sweep to complete the case study.
The strongest stimulation-associated program in the selected R K6 model is the IFN-associated pattern, labeled Pattern4 in that run. It is anchored by canonical interferon-stimulated genes, including ISG15, ISG20, IFI6, IFIT3, IFIT1, MX1, IFIT2, IRF7, OAS1, PLSCR1, and BST2.
We also performed a targeted directionality check because CoGAPS pattern weights do not by themselves indicate whether genes are up or down in stimulation. In the selected R K6 analysis, 14 of the top 15 IFN-associated pattern genes were up in IFN-beta stimulation, while FTH1 was down.
The IFN-associated pattern activity appears broad across PBMC cell types, supporting an activity-like IFN-response interpretation. Other patterns have interpretable gene anchors, such as myeloid and antigen-presentation genes, but those secondary interpretations should remain more cautious.

Before You Begin
Full reproduction uses the validated Docker image introduced in Packages and Setup. The image provides R, Python, CoGAPS, PyCoGAPS, Quarto, and the packages used by the scripts. It does not contain the project data.
Keep these three local folders distinct:

Case-study repository: the GitHub clone containing the pages, scripts, included data, and output folders.
Reproduction archive: the downloaded Zenodo or local folder containing larger source files and full saved model objects. It is mounted read-only so the downloaded files remain unchanged.
Writable work folder: a local folder for regenerated files, logs, and trial outputs.

Before starting a long run, confirm that you have enough local storage for the downloaded archive and regenerated model files. Runtime depends on the computer, Docker architecture, diagnostic settings, and thread support. The selected-model section therefore shows what progress should look like instead of promising one universal runtime.
Use the commands below from your computer’s Terminal. If you already cloned the repository, skip the git clone command and move into your existing repository folder.
# Get the case-study repository if you have not already cloned it.
git clone https://github.com/opencasestudies/ocs-bio-latent-variable.git
cd ocs-bio-latent-variable

# Point to the downloaded Zenodo or local reproduction archive.
mkdir -p "$HOME/cs4_reproduction_archive"
export CS4_REPRODUCTION_ARCHIVE="$HOME/cs4_reproduction_archive"

# Create a writable folder for regenerated outputs.
mkdir -p "$PWD/reproduction_work"

# Launch the validated case-study image.
docker run --platform linux/amd64 --rm -it \
  -p 8787:8787 \
  -e PASSWORD="Password12" \
  -v "$PWD":/home/rstudio/project:rw \
  -v "$CS4_REPRODUCTION_ARCHIVE":/home/rstudio/project/data/external/reproduction_archive:ro \
  othomas2/pycogaps-runtime-guide:0.3.0
Inside Docker, the repository appears at /home/rstudio/project, and the reproduction archive appears at /home/rstudio/project/data/external/reproduction_archive. Write regenerated files to the repository’s expected output folders or to reproduction_work/ while testing.
After the container starts, inspect the downloaded archive before copying or linking anything:
cd /home/rstudio/project
find data/external/reproduction_archive -maxdepth 5 -type f | sort

If the archive preserves those project-relative folders, copy the files you need into the matching writable locations or pass the archive path through the relevant command-line option. section: Stage 2: Rebuild The Prepared PBMC Dataset
text:
Stage 2: Rebuild The Prepared PBMC Dataset
Use this stage when you want to reconstruct the expression dataset that CoGAPS received. The source file contains the larger single-cell count dataset; the prepared file keeps the cells, metadata, normalized expression values, and 3,000 highly variable genes used in the analysis.
data/processed/input/preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad
If you already have the included prepared file and do not want to revisit preprocessing, you can continue to Stage 3. Reading the explanation is still useful because filtering, normalization, transformation, and gene selection determine the exact matrix available to the model.
The preprocessing script is:
scripts/reproduction/prepare_preprocessed_hvg3000.py
It performs six main jobs:

reads the larger source .h5ad file;
keeps a raw count layer for steps that need count-scale values;
removes genes detected in too few cells;
normalizes and log-transforms expression values;
selects 3,000 highly variable genes; and
writes both the prepared case-study data file and the optional dense PyCoGAPS input.

The recorded preprocessing workflow is implemented in Python. Run the complete script inside Docker from /home/rstudio/project after the source file is available:
/opt/cogaps-venv/bin/python scripts/reproduction/prepare_preprocessed_hvg3000.py \
  --source-h5ad data/source/kang_counts_25k.h5ad \
  --out-h5ad data/processed/input/preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad \
  --cogaps-input-h5ad data/processed/input/cogaps_input_genesxcells_hvg3000_float64.h5ad \
  --config-json data/processed/input/preprocess_config_hvg3000.json

The Script Starts By Making The Choices Visible
The first important design choice is that preprocessing settings are command-line arguments, not hidden constants. The script has defaults, but the command above could override them if you wanted to test another preprocessing recipe.
parser.add_argument("--min-cells", type=int, default=3)
parser.add_argument("--target-sum", type=float, default=10000.0)
parser.add_argument("--n-top-genes", type=int, default=3000)
parser.add_argument("--hvg-flavor", default="seurat_v3")
These four arguments describe the main preprocessing decisions:

min_cells = 3 means a gene must be detected in at least three cells to remain in the dataset.
target_sum = 10000 means each cell is rescaled to the same total expression depth before log transformation.
n_top_genes = 3000 means the prepared CoGAPS input uses 3,000 highly variable genes.
hvg_flavor = "seurat_v3" names the highly variable gene-selection method.

This is a useful reproducibility habit. If a later model result changes, you can check whether the model changed or whether the expression matrix was rebuilt with different preprocessing settings.


The Script Reads The Source AnnData File And Preserves Counts
The source file is an AnnData .h5ad object. In single-cell analysis, an AnnData object usually stores cells as rows and genes as columns. The main expression matrix is adata.X, and additional versions of the matrix can be stored in adata.layers.
The script reads the source file and makes sure there is a counts layer:
adata = ad.read_h5ad(args.source_h5ad)

if "counts" not in adata.layers:
    adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()
This matters because the workflow uses expression values in more than one way. The normalized, log-transformed matrix is easier to compare across cells and is the matrix used for the prepared case-study file. The count-scale layer is kept so highly variable gene selection can use count-like values, and so later full-reproduction steps have a clear record of where count-scale information came from.


Filtering Removes Genes With Too Little Information
The first filtering step removes genes detected in too few cells:
sc.pp.filter_genes(adata, min_cells=args.min_cells)
This step does not decide which immune cells are important. It only removes genes that are so rarely detected that they are unlikely to help the factorization. In this workflow, a gene must be detected in at least three cells. That low threshold is intentionally permissive: it removes nearly absent genes while retaining a broad expression space for the highly variable gene step.


Normalization And Log Transformation Put Cells On A Comparable Scale
Single cells can differ in total captured RNA or sequencing depth. Before comparing expression values across cells, the script rescales each cell and then log-transforms the normalized values:
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=args.target_sum)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
normalize_total() rescales each cell so that its total expression is comparable to the same target value. Here, that target is 10,000. log1p() then applies a log transform using log(1 + expression), which reduces the dominance of very large expression values while keeping zeros defined.
For this case study, the important point is not the specific number 10,000 by itself. The important point is that CoGAPS receives an expression matrix where cells have already been put on a more comparable scale.


Highly Variable Genes Define The Modeling Space
The source study measured many genes, but the selected model uses 3,000 highly variable genes. Highly variable genes are genes whose expression varies enough across cells to help distinguish cell states, cell identities, stimulation responses, or other structure.
The script marks highly variable genes, then creates a reduced AnnData object:
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(
    adata,
    n_top_genes=args.n_top_genes,
    flavor=args.hvg_flavor,
    layer="counts",
    subset=False,
)

adata_hvg = adata[:, adata.var["highly_variable"].to_numpy()].copy()
There are two small programming details worth noticing here. First, subset=False means the function adds a highly_variable column to adata.var rather than immediately dropping genes. Second, the next line uses that Boolean column as a mask to keep only the selected genes. A Boolean mask is a true/false vector: genes marked TRUE stay in adata_hvg, and genes marked FALSE are left behind.
The result is the prepared matrix used by the case study:
24,673 cells x 3,000 highly variable genes


The Script Writes Two Orientations Of The Same Prepared Data
The main prepared file is written as cells by genes, which is the usual AnnData orientation:
adata_hvg.write_h5ad(args.out_h5ad)
The script also creates an optional dense genes-by-cells file for the Python/PyCoGAPS full rerun:
def build_cogaps_input(preprocessed_cells: ad.AnnData) -> ad.AnnData:
    cogaps_input = preprocessed_cells.T.copy()
    X = cogaps_input.X.toarray() if sparse.issparse(cogaps_input.X) else cogaps_input.X
    cogaps_input.X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
    cogaps_input.var = preprocessed_cells.obs.copy()
    cogaps_input.var_names = preprocessed_cells.obs_names.astype(str).copy()
    cogaps_input.obs = preprocessed_cells.var.copy()
    cogaps_input.obs_names = preprocessed_cells.var_names.astype(str).copy()
    return cogaps_input
This function transposes the matrix so genes become rows and cells become columns. It also densifies the matrix and stores it as float64. That dense genes-by-cells file is not needed for the main analysis, but it is needed if you want to rerun the Python-compatible CoGAPS workflow with the supplied launcher.
The two outputs are therefore different views of the same prepared expression space:

preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad: cells by genes, used for the main analysis and most summaries.
cogaps_input_genesxcells_hvg3000_float64.h5ad: genes by cells, used for the optional full Python-compatible rerun.



Record The Preprocessing Choices
At the end, the script writes a compact JSON record:
config = {
    "raw_h5ad": args.source_h5ad.name,
    "min_cells": args.min_cells,
    "target_sum": args.target_sum,
    "hvg_flavor": args.hvg_flavor,
    "n_top_genes": args.n_top_genes,
    "prepared_h5ad": str(args.out_h5ad),
    "cogaps_input_h5ad": str(args.cogaps_input_h5ad),
}
args.config_json.write_text(json.dumps(config, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
After the script finishes, inspect data/processed/input/preprocess_config_hvg3000.json. That record should name the source file, minimum cell threshold, library-size target, highly variable gene method, number of selected genes, and output paths.
This file records the expression space given to CoGAPS before model interpretation begins. It answers questions such as why the selected model has 3,000 genes and whether the expression matrix was normalized before model fitting.


Check The Prepared Dataset
After preprocessing finishes, inspect the saved file in either R or Python. The two snippets check the same properties: matrix dimensions, availability of the count layer, and the cell metadata fields used later for donor-, condition-, and cell-type-aware analyses.

RPython


prepared_r <- zellkonverter::readH5AD(
  "data/processed/input/preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad"
)

data.frame(
  cells = ncol(prepared_r),
  genes = nrow(prepared_r),
  count_layer_present = "counts" %in% SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(prepared_r),
  metadata_fields = paste(
    colnames(SummarizedExperiment::colData(prepared_r)),
    collapse = ", "
  )
)


import anndata as ad

prepared_py = ad.read_h5ad(
    "data/processed/input/preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad"
)

{
    "cells": prepared_py.n_obs,
    "genes": prepared_py.n_vars,
    "count_layer_present": "counts" in prepared_py.layers,
    "metadata_fields": list(prepared_py.obs.columns),
}



The prepared dataset should contain 24,673 cells and 3,000 genes. The metadata should retain the fields needed to connect each cell with its condition, donor, annotated PBMC identity, and UMAP coordinates.


Why this step is separate


Preprocessing changes the matrix that CoGAPS sees. Keeping it in a separate script makes the sequence visible: first rebuild the prepared PBMC dataset, then fit CoGAPS, then summarize the selected model. This separation also makes it easier to check a preprocessing decision without accidentally rerunning a long model.
For a full check, compare three files together:

the source file, data/source/kang_counts_25k.h5ad;
the prepared file, data/processed/input/preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad; and
the preprocessing record, data/processed/input/preprocess_config_hvg3000.json.

Together, they tell you where the data started, what matrix the case study uses, and which preprocessing choices connect the two.


Stage 2 checkpoint: The prepared H5AD file contains 24,673 cells and 3,000 genes, the count layer is available, and the preprocessing JSON records the settings used to create it. If those checks pass, the expression data are ready for the selected-model fit.

section: Stage 3: Fit The Selected R CoGAPS Model
text:
Stage 3: Fit The Selected R CoGAPS Model
The selected R model is the primary fitted model used in the analysis. This stage runs CoGAPS and saves the complete model object. Later stages read that object to create diagnostics, compact tables, directionality summaries, and figures. Keeping model fitting separate from those later exports means you do not need to refit CoGAPS whenever you want to redraw a figure or change a summary table.
The selected R model uses:

K = 6, the selected number of CoGAPS patterns;
seed = 2, the run seed used for the selected model;
n_iter = 2000, the number of iterations per CoGAPS phase;
sparseOptimization = TRUE, the sparse-optimized model path; and
diagnostic collection, including trace output, checkpoints, snapshots, and pump samples.

The complete R output map is available below for reference. You do not need to memorize it before running the model.


Open the selected R model output map











R reproduction step


Reads


Writes


Why the output matters






Fit selected R modelrun_selected_model_r.shcogaps_run_one_singleprocess_r.R


preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad and selected model settings.


cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.rds, cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.metrics.json, checkpoint output, and runtime log messages.


Creates the full primary R CoGAPS result and records the model settings, runtime, mean chi-square, run-specific IFN-associated pattern label, and top genes.




Export R diagnosticsexport_cogaps_diagnostics_r.R


Prepared PBMC file plus the full selected R .rds object.


Trace CSV, snapshot summary, uncertainty summary, pump outputs, mean pattern assignment table, and diagnostics JSON.


Makes convergence, stability, posterior uncertainty, and diagnostic evidence inspectable without manually opening the full model object.




Export compact R analysis tablesexport_lightweight_cogaps_derivatives_r.R


Prepared PBMC file plus the full selected R .rds object.


Gene-weight matrix, cell-activity matrix, posterior SD matrices, activity-with-metadata table, top genes, pattern correlations, cell-type summaries, donor summaries, and pattern summary.


Creates the compact tables used throughout Data Import, Data Exploration, Data Visualization, and Data Analysis.




Rebuild directionality evidencepattern_directionality_analysis_r.R


Prepared expression values, selected-model top genes, donor labels, condition labels, and annotated PBMC identities.


Global and cell-type directionality tables, pattern direction summary, pseudobulk support tables, and directionality heatmap.


Shows whether high-weight pattern genes are higher or lower after IFN-beta stimulation; this prevents interpreting CoGAPS weights as expression direction.






Run The Model Where You Can See Its Progress
Run the launcher from your normal computer Terminal or from the Docker/RStudio Terminal while you can watch the output:
bash scripts/reproduction/run_selected_model_r.sh
The launcher writes selected-model outputs to:
data/processed/selected_model_k6/r/
If a full R selected-model object already exists, the launcher stops before overwriting it. To intentionally rerun the model, set FORCE_RERUN=1:
FORCE_RERUN=1 bash scripts/reproduction/run_selected_model_r.sh
The launcher checks that R CoGAPS was compiled with OpenMP support and sets OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 before starting the run. It then calls scripts/cogaps_run_one_singleprocess_r.R with the selected settings.
The R runner does four important things:

reads data/processed/input/preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad with zellkonverter;
extracts the normalized expression matrix used by CoGAPS;
builds CogapsParams() with the selected K, seed, iteration count, and sparse-optimization setting; and
saves the full CoGAPS result as cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.rds.

The log should show CoGAPS progressing through equilibration and sampling. During equilibration, the sampler moves away from its starting state and toward a region of the model space that fits the data better. During sampling, CoGAPS continues updating the model while collecting the posterior summaries used in the final result.
While the run is active, check for four signs of progress:

the input dimensions and selected settings are printed correctly;
iteration numbers continue to increase;
the run moves from equilibration into sampling; and
the final requested sampling iteration is reached without an error.

Chi-square values do not need to decrease at every sampling update. CoGAPS is a stochastic sampler rather than a monotone optimizer, so small fluctuations during the sampling phase are expected. The diagnostic exports in Stage 4 make the full trace easier to inspect.
The first files to check after this stage are the full selected R CoGAPS object, the metrics JSON, and the checkpoint file. The .rds object is the source for later exports. The metrics JSON provides a compact record of settings, runtime, dimensions, and headline model summaries. The checkpoint is mainly useful for debugging or resuming a run.
Stage 3 checkpoint: The Terminal shows that equilibration and sampling completed, and data/processed/selected_model_k6/r/ contains the full .rds model and metrics JSON. Do not continue to the export stage if the fit ended with an error or stopped before completing sampling.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Finding latent immune-response programs in single-cell RNA-seq with CoGAPS
section: Stage 4: Create Diagnostic And Analysis Tables
text:
Stage 4: Create Diagnostic And Analysis Tables
The full model object contains much more information than is practical to display directly in a web page. This stage creates smaller files for two purposes:

diagnostic tables summarize the model trace, snapshots, assignments, and posterior uncertainty;
analysis tables organize gene weights, cell activities, top genes, and grouped activity summaries into forms that can be inspected with R or Python.

These are not additional model fits. They are different views of the same selected R result.

Export Diagnostics From The Full R Model
The full .rds object is useful, but it is not the easiest format to inspect directly. The diagnostic export script reads the full result and writes smaller files that are easy to plot or summarize:
Rscript scripts/export_cogaps_diagnostics_r.R
This script reads two inputs:

data/processed/input/preprocessed_cells_hvg3000.h5ad, so it can check matrix orientation and names; and
data/processed/selected_model_k6/r/cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.rds, the full selected R CoGAPS result.

The script extracts four model matrices from the CoGAPS object:

the gene-loading matrix, often called A, where rows are genes and columns are patterns;
the cell-activity matrix, often called P, where rows are cells and columns are patterns;
the gene-loading standard-deviation matrix; and
the cell-activity standard-deviation matrix.

It also reads CoGAPS metadata: chi-square trace values, atom-count traces, snapshots, pump statistics, mean pattern assignment summaries, run parameters, and runtime metadata.
The main outputs are:









Diagnostic output


What it contains


Where it is used






cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.trace.csv


Chi-square and atom-count traces across the run.


Convergence and stability checks.




cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.snapshot_summary.csv


Comparisons between saved intermediate sampler states and the final selected result.


Snapshot-based stability checks.




cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.pattern_uncertainty_summary.csv


Per-pattern uncertainty summaries based on posterior standard-deviation matrices.


Posterior uncertainty interpretation.




cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.pump_stat.tsv.gzcogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.mean_pattern_assignment.tsv.gz


Pump and mean pattern-assignment diagnostics, when those diagnostics are present in the saved result.


Pattern assignment and diagnostic record.




cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.diagnostics.json


Compact diagnostic record with dimensions, parameter settings, trace summaries, snapshot counts, and metadata fields.


Run-level reporting and checks.




These files are the bridge between model fitting and model diagnosis. They let you check convergence, snapshots, uncertainty, and runtime without opening a large R object by hand.


Export Compact R Tables For Analysis
The next export script turns the same full R result into the matrices and summaries used throughout the main analysis sections:
Rscript scripts/export_lightweight_cogaps_derivatives_r.R
This script again reads the prepared PBMC .h5ad file and the selected R .rds object. It then creates the tables that the main analysis uses.
The export script creates three kinds of files:









Output family


Output files


How the files are used






Model matrices


pattern_gene_weights.tsv.gzpattern_cell_activities.tsv.gzpattern_gene_weight_sd.tsv.gzpattern_cell_activity_sd.tsv.gz


Gene weights identify which genes define each pattern. Cell activities identify where each pattern is used across cells. Posterior SD matrices support uncertainty summaries.




Cell activities joined to metadata


pattern_cell_activities_with_metadata.csv.gz


Joins each cell’s pattern activities to barcode, condition, donor/replicate, annotated PBMC identity, and UMAP coordinates. This is what lets later sections compare pattern activity with stimulation, cell identity, donor structure, and UMAP location.




Pattern-level summaries


pattern_top_genes.csvpattern_correlations.csvpattern_activity_by_celltype_condition.csvpattern_activity_by_replicate_condition.csvpattern_summary.csv


Ranks top genes, measures association with stimulation, summarizes activity by PBMC identity and donor, and gathers compact pattern evidence for tables and figures.




These files are not separate models. They are smaller views of the selected R model, reshaped so you can inspect one kind of evidence at a time.


Check The Exported Tables In R Or Python
The export scripts are written in R because they read the full R CoGAPS object. Once the CSV and compressed TSV files have been created, you can inspect them in either language.

RPython


pattern_summary_r <- readr::read_csv(
  "data/processed/selected_model_k6/r/pattern_summary.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

pattern_summary_r |>
  dplyr::select(
    pattern,
    corr_with_stim,
    dominant_cell_type,
    top_genes_top8
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()


import pandas as pd

pattern_summary_py = pd.read_csv(
    "data/processed/selected_model_k6/r/pattern_summary.csv"
)

pattern_summary_py[
    [
        "pattern",
        "corr_with_stim",
        "dominant_cell_type",
        "top_genes_top8",
    ]
]



Both snippets read the same R-selected-model summary. The check should return one row for each of the six patterns and retain the columns needed to connect stimulation association, cell identity, and top genes.
Stage 4 checkpoint: The trace, uncertainty, gene-weight, cell-activity, top-gene, and pattern-summary files are present. The pattern summary contains six rows, and the matrices retain matching gene, cell, and pattern labels.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Finding latent immune-response programs in single-cell RNA-seq with CoGAPS
text:
Stage 5: Rebuild Directionality And Figures
The selected-model exports show which genes have high CoGAPS weights and where each pattern is active. They do not show whether a high-weight gene increases or decreases after IFN-beta stimulation. This stage adds that expression-direction evidence and rebuilds the figures that display the combined results.

Rebuild Directionality Evidence
The R model export tells you which genes have high CoGAPS weights. It does not tell you whether those genes are higher after IFN-beta stimulation. Directionality is rebuilt with a separate expression-contrast script. Choose the command that matches the selected-model outputs you are rebuilding.

RPython


Rscript scripts/pattern_directionality_analysis_r.R


/opt/cogaps-venv/bin/python scripts/pattern_directionality_analysis.py



This script uses the prepared expression values, selected model top genes, donor labels, condition labels, and annotated PBMC identities. It builds pseudobulk summaries and compares IFN-beta-stimulated aliquots with matched control aliquots.
The main outputs are:









Directionality output


What it contains


Why it matters






pattern_gene_directionality_global.csv


Gene-level IFN-beta versus control contrasts across all cells.


Checks whether top genes rise or fall overall.




pattern_gene_directionality_by_celltype.csv


Gene-level contrasts within annotated PBMC identities.


Checks whether direction is consistent or cell-type-specific.




pattern_direction_summary.csv


One row per pattern summarizing how many top genes are higher or lower after stimulation.


Supports pattern-level direction interpretation.




pseudobulk_counts_global.csvpseudobulk_counts_by_celltype.csv


Support files showing how many observations contributed to the expression summaries.


Helps check whether a contrast is based on enough cells.




pattern_gene_directionality_heatmap.png


Compact visual summary of directionality across patterns and cell types.


Useful for quick review after rerunning the directionality script.




The directionality step is part of the evidence chain because CoGAPS weights and expression fold-changes answer different questions. A gene can strongly define a pattern and still move in either direction after stimulation. The case study therefore interprets gene weights and expression direction together.


Check The R Output Folder
After running the R fit and export scripts, inspect the output folder:
find data/processed/selected_model_k6/r -maxdepth 1 -type f | sort
You should see the full selected model, diagnostic files, lightweight matrices, activity summaries, top-gene tables, and directionality summaries. If a later case-study section cannot find a file, start by checking whether it appears in this folder and whether it was regenerated after the latest model run.


Regenerate The Displayed Figures
Most displayed figures are built from processed evidence tables rather than directly from a live model fit. That separation makes it possible to update a visualization without waiting for CoGAPS to run again.
Regenerate the shared selected-model figures with:
/opt/cogaps-venv/bin/python scripts/build_selected_k6_figures.py
The script writes figures under data/processed/figures/ and updates selected display copies under img/. Figures generated directly by R and Python code chunks are refreshed when the complete Quarto page is rendered:
quarto render
Before interpreting a rebuilt figure, confirm that its source table was regenerated from the same selected-model output. A newly rendered image does not correct an older source table by itself.
Stage 5 checkpoint: Directionality tables and pseudobulk support files are present for the selected output, the expected figures have been regenerated, and the Quarto render completes without missing-file errors.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Finding latent immune-response programs in single-cell RNA-seq with CoGAPS
text:
Stage 6: Confirm The Reproduction
A successful script exit is necessary, but it is not the only check. Confirm that the regenerated files still represent the intended dataset and model.








Check
Expected result
Why it matters




Prepared data
24,673 cells, 3,000 genes, and the required condition, donor, cell-type, and UMAP fields
Confirms that CoGAPS received the intended cells, genes, and metadata.


Selected settings
K = 6, seed 2, 2,000 iterations per phase, and sparse optimization enabled
Confirms that the regenerated model matches the selected specification.


Pattern structure
Six gene-weight and cell-activity columns with aligned pattern labels
Confirms that the compact exports describe the complete selected model.


Diagnostics
Trace, snapshot, uncertainty, metrics, and available pump files are present for R
Confirms that the evidence needed to evaluate the R run was exported.


Directionality
Global, cell-type, paired, and pseudobulk support tables are present
Confirms that expression direction can be interpreted separately from CoGAPS weights.


Display files
Figures were rebuilt after their source tables
Confirms that the page displays the current evidence.



The checks below summarize the selected-model folder from either language. They do not decide whether the biological interpretation is correct; they confirm that the expected evidence files are available and internally complete.

RPython


r_dir <- "data/processed/selected_model_k6/r"

r_check <- data.frame(
  check = c(
    "pattern rows",
    "trace file",
    "uncertainty file",
    "directionality file",
    "full R model"
  ),
  value = c(
    nrow(readr::read_csv(file.path(r_dir, "pattern_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)),
    file.exists(file.path(r_dir, "cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.trace.csv")),
    file.exists(file.path(r_dir, "cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.pattern_uncertainty_summary.csv")),
    file.exists(file.path(r_dir, "pattern_gene_directionality_global.csv")),
    file.exists(file.path(r_dir, "cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.rds"))
  )
)

knitr::kable(r_check)


from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

py_dir = Path("data/processed/selected_model_k6/python")

py_check = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "check": [
            "pattern rows",
            "metrics file",
            "directionality file",
            "full Python-compatible model",
        ],
        "value": [
            len(pd.read_csv(py_dir / "pattern_summary.csv")),
            (py_dir / "cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.metrics.json").exists(),
            (py_dir / "pattern_gene_directionality_global.csv").exists(),
            (py_dir / "cogaps_K6_seed2_iter2000.h5ad").exists(),
        ],
    }
)

py_check



The R table should report six pattern rows and TRUE for every expected file. The Python table should also report six pattern rows and TRUE for its available output files. The Python list is shorter because the Python-compatible run does not expose the same snapshot and pump diagnostics as the selected R run.
If a regenerated value differs, stop before replacing the included evidence. Review the preprocessing record, matrix orientation, model settings, random seed, runtime environment, and export logs to identify where the difference entered the workflow.
Stage 6 checkpoint: The structural checks pass, the expected files are current, and any differences from the included result have been explained before the regenerated files are used for interpretation.
